intro: Rachmaninoff plays his Prelude in G♯ minor, Op. 32 No. 12, in which a left-hand melody sounds beneath quick, circling notes. The hands exchange roles in the middle section, and the short figures continue until close to the end.

sections.label: A · Right-hand figuration over left-hand melody
sections.mNote: The right hand plays figuration while the left plays the melody.

sections.label: B · Melody in upper register
sections.mNote: Running notes in the left hand accompany the upper melody

sections.label: A′ · The circling figure again
sections.mNote: The upper notes resume above the lower tune

sections.label: Coda · Meno mosso, then perdendo
sections.mNote: The figures slow and fade towards G♯.

cues.title: Left-hand melody
cues.text: The right hand opens alone with a circling semiquaver figure. Beneath it, the left hand begins a melody in longer notes, while the right-hand semiquavers continue above.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition (1911), p. 48: Allegro in 12/8, right-hand semiquavers and the later left-hand melodic entry. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e0/IMSLP105591-PMLP02018-Rachmaninov_-_32_-_13_Preludes_(ed.Gutheil).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Middle passage, melody in right hand
cues.text: In the middle passage the melody moves up into the right hand, over running semiquavers in the left. The intervals widen, and chords fill out the line as the piano grows louder.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 49–50: upper melody over left-hand semiquavers, followed by the expanding chordal passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the semiquaver figure
cues.text: The upper semiquaver figure returns above the lower melody. As before, Rachmaninoff divides the hands sharply. One hand plays the melody in long notes, and the other repeats a figure on a few pitches. The music rises once more to ff before the close.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 50, latter systems: the upper semiquaver figure returns, with a lower melody and a further rise to ff.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing page, meno mosso
cues.text: The closing page is marked meno mosso, then perdendo. The right hand continues its small figures over held bass notes and climbs briefly into a high register. Both hands then descend to the final G♯.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 51: meno mosso, held bass notes, the high octave passage and final perdendo to G♯.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Melody and accompaniment change hands
transitions.from: A · Right-hand figuration over left-hand melody
transitions.how: The piano’s circling semiquaver figure passes into the left hand beneath a sustained right-hand melody. The bass now plays the semiquavers that first sounded above the tune. As the melody climbs, it fills out into chords, with a crescendo.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 49–50: exchange of the melody and semiquaver accompaniment, followed by the chordal expansion.

transitions.title: Return of the upper semiquaver figure
transitions.how: After the broad chords, the right hand returns to its small semiquaver figure, with the melody below it. As at the opening, the texture is divided between a singing line and quick notes. The dynamic falls, then builds towards another fortissimo.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 50, latter systems: restored upper figuration, lower melody and renewed ff.

transitions.title: Meno mosso, a tempo and perdendo
transitions.how: At meno mosso the bass holds long notes under the piano’s continuing figures in the upper register. On the last page the original tempo returns briefly, marked a tempo in the Gutheil first edition. The figures rise into high octaves, then descend under perdendo. The piece ends on G♯.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 51: meno mosso, sustained bass, a tempo and final perdendo.

fields.note: Victor’s contemporary 1925 catalogue lists this Prelude on record 812, which DAHR maps to the same B-24642 take 5 as the earlier single-faced 64963. This establishes publication no later than 1925, independently of the 1921 session date, and eligibility under the project’s pre-1926 US recording rule. The exact first-publication day remains unknown. The 1992 booklet retains an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any unidentified new creative contribution to the mastering is independently cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
